newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Many Bosnian refugees decline chance to go home.
newsitem.headline: Many Bosnian refugees decline chance to go home.

text.p: Bosnians went to the polls on Saturday in elections aimed at healing the divisions of war, but thousands of refugees appeared to have passed up the chance of voting in their former home towns under NATO protection.

Nearly three million Bosnians, including several hundred thousand refugees, were entitled to vote in elections for joint institutions which international organisers hope will spur reunification of the shattered country.

But by early afternoon only a few thousand refugees were reported to have crossed ethnic borders, along 19 designated routes guarded by NATO-led peace troops, to cast their vote in home towns from which they fled or were expelled.

A spokesman for the peace force said that by 2.30 p.m. local time a total of 142 buses carrying refugee voters had crossed internal borders within Bosnia, and a further 50 were on the road. Organisers had forecast some 140,000 refugees would be on the move on Saturday.
Since the cancellation of planned municipal elections due to irregularities in registering refugee voters, there was little incentive for refugees to risk going back.
They are able to record their votes for a collective presidency and parliament as well as assemblies for a Moslem-Croat federation and a Serb republic by absentee ballot.
Arrangements were made for up to 8,000 Moslems to be taken by bus to Serb-held Srebrenica in eastern Bosnia, but by midday only a handful had turned up.
Several hundred Moslem refugees crossed into Doboj in northern Bosnia, a former Moslem-majority town now under Serb control.

Voting got off to a shaky start after over 4,000 polling stations opened at 7 a.m. (0500 GMT), with early reports of a shooting attack on a Sarajevo polling station and Serbs blocking a route chosen for refugees.

But later the Organisation of Security and Cooperation in Europe, organising the poll, said the blockage around Prijedor in northern Bosnia was mainly due to traffic problems caused by too many private cars.
International organisers also reported that three buses taking refugees to vote were stoned between Mostar and Capljina, in Croat-controlled territory in the south-west, but nobody was injured.
The head of the OSCE mission to Bosnia, Robert Frowick, told Bosnian radio in the early afternoon: "We have to expect some incidents and problems, but overall things are going pretty well."
Serb refugees arrived in Bosnia through the night, brought by train from Belgrade to vote in the Bosnian Serb Republic.
The biggest short-term fear of the international community was of violence between ethnic rivals meeting one another on Saturday in places they once fought over.

The United States has led a chorus of senior Western officials in publicly proclaiming the country has no choice but to go through with the elections, however flawed, if it is ever to recover from the conflict.
